text:
The federal government has acquired a 43.6-acre complex on Route 50 in Falls Church from GBA Associates for $285 million, the Washington Business Journal reported on Sept. 25.

The property, at 7700 Arlington Blvd., serves as the headquarters of the Defense Health Agency, which provides healthcare to members of the military and their families and operates over 700 hospitals and clinics across the world.

The fee-simple acquisition was handled for the federal government by the Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command. The National Capital Planning Commission had no problems with the sale when it was previewed at the NCPS’s meeting in July, according to the WBJ.

The complex formerly housed the Raytheon Corp.

The Defense Health Agency has occupied the property since 2011, after signing a 15-year, $370 million lease. It was the largest lease signed in Northern Virginia in 2010, the WBJ reports. The deal was part of the Base Realignment and Closure process that forced the military’s healthcare providers to consolidate from 14 locations across the country.

The campus has three office buildings with a total of 686,000 square feet and 2,000 parking spaces.

FALLS CHURCH, Virginia – The Defense Health Agency announced that TRICARE beneficiaries in two West Virginia counties may receive emergency prescription refills now through Oct. 4, due to flooding.

The counties affected are Boone and Lincoln.

To receive an emergency refill of prescription medications, TRICARE beneficiaries should take their prescription bottle to any TRICARE retail network pharmacy. If the bottle is unavailable or the label is damaged or missing, beneficiaries should contact Express Scripts, Inc., or their retail network pharmacy for assistance.

To find a network pharmacy, beneficiaries may call Express Scripts at 1-877-363-1303, or search the https://militaryrx.express-scripts.com/find-pharmacy.

If possible, visit the pharmacy where the prescription was filled. Prescriptions filled by a retail chain may be filled at another store in that chain. If the clinician who prescribed the medication is available, beneficiaries can ask them to call in a new prescription to any network pharmacy.

As a reminder, TRICARE beneficiaries, other than active duty service members, may receive urgent care from any TRICARE-authorized urgent care center or provider and do not need a referral. This allows beneficiaries to seek nonemergency care for illnesses or injuries if their primary care provider is unavailable because of emergencies. Any TRICARE beneficiary who reasonably believes they have an emergency should always call 911 or, go to the nearest emergency room.

Beneficiaries are advised to visit Express Scripts’ https://militaryrx.express-scripts.com/notices/weather/2026-sep-24/state-emergency-alert-flooding-west-virginia for updates.

text:
Who Wants To Be A Billionaire? Just bill Medicaid and Medicare.

Luke Rosiak•Sep 29, 2026

Your browser does not support the audio element.

Bernie Sanders may believe billionaires shouldn’t exist, but the government healthcare programs he wants to expand are so easy to defraud that even unsophisticated criminals are joining the three-comma club.

Medicaid and Medicare billing are a world where Russian mobsters can simply submit bills for $10 billion in urinary catheters, and $1 billion will be paid out. That’s led to the rise of a new phenomenon: the billion-dollar government fraudster, according to a new report on “the new robber barons” from Sen. Joni Ernst (R-Iowa), who chairs the Senate DOGE Caucus.

They include an illegal immigrant who billed Medicare $1.3 billion in six months (he’s still at large), a Filipina nurse who billed $906 million to Medicare and the military’s health plan (she’s free on bail in the United States as she awaits trial), and a Phoenix socialite couple who billed $1.2 billion by performing unneeded treatments on people in hospice (they were wearing $30,000 watches when they were arrested).

Kansas man Brett Blackman posed outside his mansion wearing a gold dollar-sign necklace after billing the government more than $1 billion for orthotic braces and other unnecessary equipment for old people, using foreign call centers and fake doctors’ notes. Half of the billion was paid out before he was convicted in May. Prosecutors said Blackman owned DMERx, an “internet-based platform that generated false and fraudulent doctors’ orders for durable medical equipment (DME) and prescriptions for other items. As part of the scheme, Blackman and his co-conspirators connected pharmacies, DME suppliers, and marketers with telemedicine companies that would accept illegal kickbacks and bribes in exchange for signed doctors’ orders.”

Phoenix socialite Alexandra Gehrke and her husband “DJ Jeffrey” King submitted $1.2 billion in claims for “expensive, medically unnecessary” wound grafts for people in hospice. The claims were submitted to Medicare, the military’s TRICARE, and CHAMPVA, a program for the family members of disabled veterans. They bought $1 million in cars, including a Ferrari 488 Spider convertible, along with a $6 million mansion and $10,000 gold cigarette lighter. They were wearing $30,000 watches when they were arrested at an airport in 2024.

A nurse from the Philippines, Marizel Yukee, did the same, billing up to $1 million per patient for wound treatments for people on their deathbeds. She was charged with billing $906 million to Medicare and TRICARE. She planned a $5 million beach resort in the Philippines and bought an $865,000 Bulgari necklace. Some wounds were allowed to be infected, while in other cases, surgeries were performed on wounds that had already healed. She was indicted in Houston in June and allowed to remain in her home while awaiting trial.

Brian Rowan also allegedly got in on the “wound care” grift, scheming to defraud government healthcare programs of $1.2 billion, often by giving people dying in hospice care unnecessary skin treatments. $614 million was paid out over three years before he was charged in June.

Illegal alien Erekle Gugava submitted at least $1.3 billion in fraudulent claims to Medicare in just five months, and laundered $7 million to the Russian mob before fleeing the country. He billed for nonexistent services by stealing the identities of elderly Americans. The scheme was flagged thanks to people who reported receiving government benefits reports showing equipment and doctors visits that they had never heard of. Gugava is still at large.

Another gang of Russian mobsters absconded with almost $1 billion after submitting more than $10 billion in invoices to Medicare for urinary catheters, using the stolen identities of doctors and senior citizens.

Ibrahim Khaldoon Hilmi led a gang of foreigners who submitted $3.7 billion in fake claims for orthotic braces, glucose monitors, and wound dressings. They successfully obtained $5.7 million, and Hilmi fled to Turkey, where he was arrested.

Herbert Leon Kimble used foreign call centers to pester elderly and disabled Americans into accepting $1.2 billion in “free or low-cost” back, shoulder, wrist, or knee braces that they didn’t need, and which were billed to Medicare. The feds paid $200 million, which they laundered through foreign corporations to purchase yachts and luxury real estate. Kimble was captured in the Philippines in June.

A CNBC story quoted a former Medicare fraudster in Florida saying “It’s just so easy. It’s unbelievable.” It said Medicare spends $901 billion a year and Medicaid spends $734 billion, yet the Department of Health and Human Services Inspector General has only 450 agents looking for fraud. At least $100 billion a year, and probably much more, is stolen, experts said.

Ernst said the inability of government healthcare programs to stop paying scam, fly-by-night companies hundreds of millions of dollars shows how the “Medicare for All” pushed by Democratic Socialists would turn out.

“Washington is literally making these scammers instant billionaires off the backs of the working class. Yet, you never hear socialists ranting about this unfair redistribution of wealth,” she said. “When the socialists demand ‘Medicare for All,’ apparently they really mean it, even if that includes Russian mobsters.”

She said the eye-popping totals highlight the need to pass her Protecting American Taxpayers Act, which would require payments to be made as reimbursements after a service is already completed, bar people convicted of defrauding the government from receiving future assistance, and pay bonuses to government auditors who find fraud.

Overview

Physician (Internal Medicine) Joint Base San Antonio

Time to invest in some new footwear because if you're San Antonio-bound, you'd better show up in boots! The Alamo City is one of the military's most envied postings and is often referred to as "Military City USA". Low cost of living, affordable homes, and the lack of state tax on retirement income are a few financial perks to living and retiring in this Texas city. A robust job market that seems partial to government and defense/security contracting ensures employment opportunities for spouses or transitioning service members. San Antonio is the country's seventh fastest growing city yet has somehow managed to retain a "small town feel." Quality schools and friendly locals (most with military ties) are additional perks to living in San Antonio.

Some things you should know before you get here: trucks are the norm (the bigger, the better), love for The Spurs (NBA) runs deep, the H-E-B obsession is real (it's a grocery store), rodeos are life, and don't call it "San Antone"-that's just wrong. The community boasts a vibrant Hispanic population, and enhances everything from the food, to the music, to community events. You don't necessarily need to speak Spanish to get around, but you'd better know how to say barbacoa, tamales, and cascarones.

Name brand shopping (IKEA is the latest arrival of note), restaurants, and all variety of entertainment all add to San Antonio's quality of life. SeaWorld, the San Antonio Zoo, Six Flags Fiesta Texas, and downtown museums are all fun outings for kids and families. Tube or kayak down a river, play or fish in the lakes, or relax by San Antonio's famous downtown River Walk. Museums, art galleries, and historical landmarks-remember The Alamo?-round out San Antonio's cultural offerings. Tex-mex cuisine arguably originated here, and some up and coming culinary trendsetters are making a name for themselves in the Pearl District downtown, alongside several notable breweries.

San Antonio has over 300 days of sunshine with some hot summers, mild winters and pleasant spring and fall seasons. San Antonio is in Bexar County (it's pronounced "BEAR") in south central Texas, and is just south of the gorgeous Hill Country. It's only about two hours from Austin, the beach, or the desert.

Works under the supervision of the Chief, Internal Medicine Service, who discusses policies and objectives. Daily work involves management of complicated medical problems such congestive heart failure, valvular heart disease, hypertension, peptic ulcer disease, thyroid disorders, diabetes, arthritic conditions etc. Examines patients, takes histories, performs physical examinations, orders laboratory tests, makes definitive diagnoses and prescribes treatment to meet needs of patients, and refers as appropriate to specialty/subspecialty care. Follows full care of all patients and insures return from consultant. Admits patients to the hospital when appropriate. Monitors and manages care for patients as they move through the system to ensure cost effective care.

Notifies patients of abnormal reports. Performs outpatient procedures to include graded exercise tests.

Serves as an inpatient general medicine ward attending physician. Must be available for telephonic or personal consultation for inpatient care when on call.

Responsible for consultative preoperative and perioperative recommendations to the surgical specialties in BAMC, as well as teaching consultative medicine to the housestaff assigned to his/her rotation. Attends Continuing Medical Education (CME) Courses and maintains specialty specific CME sufficient to satisfy the requirement of applicable licensing agencies and the Joint Commission on the Accreditation of Healthcare Organizations.

Performs other duties as assigned.

text:
A federal jury in Fort Worth convicted a Texas-licensed professional counselor of orchestrating a $26 million scheme involving fraud, kickbacks and money laundering tied to the military’s TRICARE health insurance program, the Justice Department announced.

Kevin D. Curry, 64, of Frisco, was found guilty of three counts of health care fraud, three counts of offering and paying illegal health care kickbacks, and three counts of engaging in monetary transactions in criminally derived property. He faces a maximum of 10 years in prison on each count. The department did not announce a sentencing date. A federal judge will determine his sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Curry owned and operated two purported mental health clinics in Texas, Acuity TMS of Plano and Acuity TMS of Fort Worth, and one in Florida, Emerald Coast TMS of Fort Walton Beach. The operation billed TRICARE for transcranial magnetic stimulation therapy that was medically unnecessary or never provided, prosecutors said.

Curry paid more than $5.5 million in kickbacks to persuade active-duty servicemembers, veterans and their relatives to consent to treatment for which they did not qualify and, in many cases, did not receive, according to the department. Curry falsely presented himself as a medical doctor and used physicians’ credentials without their knowledge or consent to submit claims. To conceal the scheme, he directed employees to fabricate medical records that were submitted to TRICARE, prosecutors said.

The clinics billed TRICARE more than $26 million in false, fraudulent and kickback-tainted claims, and the program paid approximately $17 million, according to the department. Curry laundered some of the proceeds by spending them on hotels, a casino-themed party and a gold-plated Tesla Cybertruck worth more than $100,000.

Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division said Curry exploited a health care program serving active-duty servicemembers and their families. The department “will continue to aggressively pursue anyone who abuses federal programs for personal gain,” he said.

U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould of the Northern District of Texas said Curry “shamelessly preyed on the trust of servicemembers, veterans, and their families.”

The Defense Criminal Investigative Service, the FBI, the Texas Attorney General’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit and the Department of Veterans Affairs Office of Inspector General investigated. Assistant U.S. Attorney Ethan Womble and Justice Department trial attorneys Adam Tisdall and Yael Mash are prosecuting the case.

text:
The Defense Health Agency seeks industry input on hosting data from vendor and VA applications

The RFI explores DHA-managed, cloud, vendor-hosted, hybrid and federated data models

Responses to DHA’s sources-sought notice are due Oct. 26

The Defense Health Agency is seeking industry input through a request for information on hosting, integrating, securing and sustaining data for the Operational Brain Health Assessment Tool/Brain Health Assessment System, or OBHAT/BHAS, program. The effort supports the Warfighter Readiness, Performance and Brain Health Project Management Office, and DHA said responses will inform a future data hosting strategy.

As DHA charts its next data hosting strategy, join the agency’s leaders and other federal health officials at the Potomac Officers Club’s 2026 Healthcare Summit on Dec. 3 in McLean, Virginia. Hear firsthand how DHA, the Department of Health and Human Services and the Veterans Health Administration plan to acquire digital tools and AI, strengthen data privacy and shape their fiscal 2027 contracting priorities. Reserve your spot and connect with the people shaping the future of federal healthcare.

What Hosting Models Is DHA Considering for OBHAT/BHAS Data?

According to the solicitation posted on SAM.gov, the market research covers data that vendor-developed and Department of Veterans Affairs applications generate. DHA, which operates within the Department of War, said it lacks a finalized enterprise strategy for how it will host, govern, integrate, retain and access that data.

The agency invites input on several models, including:

DHA-managed environments

Department of War enterprise cloud and authorized commercial cloud

Vendor-hosted software-as-a-service or platform-as-a-service offerings

Hybrid architectures

Federated or virtualized data-access models

For each model, respondents should identify the hosting location, ownership model, government and contractor responsibilities, advantages, disadvantages and potential migration barriers. The notice follows DHA’s March launch of a Data and Innovation Strategy focused on strengthening how the agency manages information across military health operations.

What Data Integration Capabilities Does DHA Want?

DHA asked respondents to describe how their solutions would ingest, normalize, exchange and reconcile data from multiple vendor and VA-connected applications. The architecture should accommodate structured, semi-structured and unstructured data spanning clinical, administrative, operational, financial, scheduling, encounter and assessment records.

The agency listed integration patterns including application programming interfaces, event-based integration, secure file transfer and batch processing, along with HL7, Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources and other healthcare data interoperability standards. Respondents should also address metadata management, data lineage, error handling and master patient index or identity-matching capabilities.

How Will DHA Protect and Retain Control of OBHAT/BHAS Data?

The program involves sensitive health and personally identifiable information. Respondents should describe their role-based access controls, identity and credential management, continuous security monitoring and encryption for data at rest and in transit.

DHA also seeks governance and portability models that preserve its access to raw data, normalized data, metadata and audit logs without creating unnecessary duplication or vendor lock-in.

The RFI asks about legal-hold, retention and archival capabilities, government purpose rights and processes for transferring data to DHA or a successor system if a vendor, application or contract changes.

When Are Responses Due for the DHA Data Hosting RFI?

Responses are due by noon ET on Oct. 26. Submissions should include an executive summary of no more than two pages, a technical response, a notional architecture diagram, past-performance summaries, rough-order-of-magnitude cost information and a recommended implementation timeline. Submissions must be sent to Bryan Heickman at bryan.g.heickman.civ@health.mil.

An accompanying Minimum Essential Characteristics table from the WRPBH PMO asks respondents to evaluate whether their solutions meet minimum or desired levels across 14 characteristics, including data volume, recovery, portability, governance and sustainment. Medical R&D Contracting Division 2 at Fort Detrick, Maryland, handles the contracting activity with no set-aside used. Following response evaluations, DHA plans to set the opportunity to inactive on Nov. 10.

text:
For many uniformed service couples, celebrating a service birthday is more than marking a date on the calendar. Birthday balls, ceremonies, traditions, and gatherings have long been important parts of service life, shared with spouses and families.

For a surviving spouse, the loss of a loved one can also mean unexpectedly losing some of those traditions and connections to the military community. A birthday celebration that was once a special evening together might suddenly raise a different question: Where is my place now?

Some surviving spouses continue to attend service birthday celebrations, while others might find it difficult to return or wonder where they will fit in. Finding the right organization, unit, installation, or group can provide an opportunity to reconnect. Sometimes it simply takes time to once again find “a place at the table.” Remembering and celebrating a spouse’s service birthday can be a small, meaningful way to maintain that connection and continue the tradition that was once shared.

[SURVIVING SPOUSE CORNER: Strengthening Emotional Well-Being]

Many of you know that Nov. 10 is the Marine Corps’ birthday — complete with ceremonies, cake cutting, and “Happy Birthday, Marine!” But what about the other branches? Each service has its own special day, full of history, traditions, and pride. Here’s when and why they celebrate — and how long they’ve been serving our nation.

Army: The nation’s oldest military branch was established on June 14, 1775, a year before the Declaration of Independence. The Continental Congress created the Continental Army to coordinate the colonies' military efforts against Great Britain during the Revolutionary War. Today, the Army celebrates its birthday with ceremonies, historical displays, and, of course, cake.

Navy: Just months after the Army was formed, the Continental Congress authorized the purchase of ships to disrupt British supply lines — a move that marked Oct. 13, 1775, as the Navy’s official birthday. Though the Navy was disbanded after the Revolution, it was reestablished in 1794. The modern Navy celebrates with fleet-wide observances, balls, and heritage events.

[SURVIVING SPOUSE CORNER: The Value of Connection]

Marine Corps: Formed at Tun Tavern in Philadelphia (yes, a real tavern), the Continental Marines were established on Nov. 10, 1775, as naval infantry. The date was restored as the official birthday in 1921 by Marine Corps Order No. 47. Marines worldwide honor it with a traditional cake-cutting ceremony, a reading of the 1921 order, and a birthday message from the commandant.

Air Force: While airpower existed before World War II, it wasn’t until the National Security Act of 1947 that the U.S. Air Force became a separate branch, distinct from the Army Air Forces. The Air Force celebrates Sept. 18 with base events, flyovers, and heritage displays.

Coast Guard: The Coast Guard traces its origins to the Revenue Cutter Service, established on Aug. 4, 1790, by Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton to enforce tariffs and prevent smuggling. Over time, it merged with the U.S. Life-Saving Service to form today’s Coast Guard — a unique organization that serves both military and law enforcement roles.

Space Force: The newest branch of the armed forces was established on Dec. 20, 2019, when the FY 2020 National Defense Authorization Act was signed into law. The Space Force organizes, trains, and equips forces to protect U.S. interests in space. Its birthday is celebrated with ceremonies and STEM outreach events.

[RELATED: Space Force to Add 10,000 Guardians in Next 5 Years]

U.S. Public Health Service Commissioned Corps: Although its origins are traced to the Marine Hospital Service of 1798, the Commissioned Corps was formally established on Jan. 4, 1889, as a uniformed service dedicated to public health. Officers serve in roles spanning health, science, and engineering across the nation and abroad, often alongside other armed services during emergencies.

FORT LEAVENWORTH, Kansas — Munson Army Health Center Soldiers and civilian staff supported Fort Leavenworth Retiree Appreciation Day on Sept. 26 at the Lewis and Clark Center, connecting military retirees and their eligible family members with health screenings, information and services available through the military health system.

Col. Tiffany R. Bilderback, Munson Army Health Center director, served as a guest speaker during the opening ceremony and thanked retirees and their families for their service and continued contributions to the Army community.

“Your service strengthened our Army. Your sacrifices helped protect our nation. Your example inspired those who followed,” Bilderback said. “Although your active service may be complete, your place in the Army family is enduring.”

Following her remarks, Bilderback answered questions from the audience on a variety of topics including Munson Pharmacy services, how long dependent children remain eligible for TRICARE, and the health center’s hours and services.

Eligible beneficiaries may have covered prescriptions from military or civilian providers filled at the Munson Pharmacy at no cost when the medication is available through the military pharmacy. Regular TRICARE coverage generally continues until a dependent child turns 21, or age 23 for a qualifying full-time college student. Eligible young adults may purchase TRICARE Young Adult coverage until age 26.

Bilderback encouraged beneficiaries to obtain current information from Munson’s official website athttps://munson.tricare.miland the health center’s official Facebook page athttps://www.facebook.com/munsonhealth, noting that online search results and unofficial sources may be inaccurate or outdated.

She shared an example of an individual who recently arrived at the health center at 6 a.m. to use the pharmacy after an AI-generated search result incorrectly indicated that the pharmacy opened at that time.

“Please, if you have questions or need information, use our official sources for the most accurate information,” Bilderback said.

Many retirees age 65 and older receive their routine and specialty health care from civilian TRICARE-network providers in the surrounding community because their evolving health care needs may require access to a broader range of specialty services and clinicians with expertise in caring for older adults. Retiree Appreciation Day provided an opportunity to review resources available to them through Munson, including pharmacy services and the Armed Forces Wellness Center.

During the event, Munson team members offered blood pressure checks and oral health screenings and shared information about mental health resources. Representatives also discussed services available through the Armed Forces Wellness Center, which eligible retirees may use for health coaching, body composition testing and other wellness support.

Munson also provided a limited number of seasonal influenza vaccinations during the event. The high-dose influenza vaccine intended for beneficiaries age 65 and older had not yet arrived, but team members administered the standard-dose vaccine to eligible participants younger than 65 and to others when medically appropriate.

Retirees and their eligible family members who would still like to receive a flu vaccine may attend one of Munson’s upcoming outreach events at Frontier Chapel, located at 625 Thomas Ave., Fort Leavenworth:

Oct. 2, noon to 4 p.m.

Oct. 16, noon to 4 p.m.

Oct. 27, 2 to 6 p.m.

Nov. 6, noon to 4 p.m.

Nov. 20, noon to 4 p.m.

Munson will notify the community when the high-dose vaccine for beneficiaries age 65 and older and those with certain chronic conditions becomes available.

The health fair reflected Munson’s continued commitment to helping retirees and their families remain connected to the military health resources and benefits they have earned.

text:
For many military spouses, one of the biggest concerns during divorce is whether they'll lose their health insurance. The answer depends on several factors, including the length of the marriage, the service member's military career and how long the marriage overlapped with creditable military service.

For most former spouses, TRICARE eligibility ends when the divorce becomes final. However, some former spouses may remain eligible under federal rules that provide continued coverage after divorce.

Understanding how TRICARE eligibility may change before finalizing a divorce can help military families make informed decisions and prepare for potential changes in health coverage.

Does Divorce Automatically End TRICARE Coverage?

For most former spouses, yes. TRICARE states that a former spouse's benefits generally end on the date of divorce or annulment unless the former spouse meets specific eligibility requirements. Separation alone does not end a spouse's TRICARE eligibility.

Two rules are especially important for military spouses facing divorce: The 20/20/20 Rule and the 20/20/15 Rule. Eligibility can change based on circumstances, including remarriage or coverage under an employer-sponsored health plan. Military spouses should verify their individual eligibility instead of assuming coverage will continue after divorce.

The 20/20/20 Rule

A former spouse can remain eligible for TRICARE if:

The marriage lasted at least 20 years.

The service member completed at least 20 years of creditable service toward retirement pay.

At least 20 years of the marriage overlapped with that creditable military service.

A qualifying former spouse may continue receiving TRICARE benefits as long as the eligibility requirements continue to be met.

The 20/20/15 Rule

A former spouse could qualify for temporary TRICARE coverage when:

The marriage lasted at least 20 years.

The service member completed at least 20 years of creditable service toward retirement pay.

At least 15 years of the marriage overlapped with creditable military service.

For divorces occurring on or after Sept. 29, 1988, qualifying former spouses generally remain eligible for TRICARE for one year from the date of divorce or annulment.

When Should Military Families Start Planning?

Health insurance is one of several financial issues that should be addressed early in a military divorce. Before finalizing a divorce, consider:

Reviewing current TRICARE eligibility.

Determining whether the 20/20/20 or 20/20/15 rule may apply.

Understanding when current coverage could end.

Exploring alternative health insurance options if necessary.

Gathering information about other military benefits that may be affected.

After a divorce is finalized, the sponsor must update the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System (DEERS). Former spouses who qualify for continued TRICARE coverage also need to establish their eligibility under their own record.

What Other Military Benefits May Change?

TRICARE is only one benefit military families may need to consider. Depending on the circumstances, divorce can also raise questions involving:

Commissary privileges

Exchange privileges

Military identification cards

Survivor Benefit Plan elections

Housing allowances

Military retirement benefits

Looking at these benefits together can help give families a more complete understanding of how divorce may affect their long-term financial planning, including how military retirement benefits may be divided in a Texas divorce.

Military families evaluating the financial impact of divorce could also benefit from understanding how military allowances and compensation are treated during divorce.

What if You No Longer Qualify for TRICARE?

Losing TRICARE does not necessarily mean a former spouse immediately loses health insurance. Depending on eligibility and individual circumstances, options may include:

Continued Health Care Benefit Program (CHCBP) coverage

Health insurance through an employer

Coverage through the Health Insurance Marketplace

Other available private or public health plans

CHCBP provides temporary premium-based coverage for certain people who lose TRICARE eligibility. Qualifying former spouses generally must purchase CHCBP within 60 days of losing TRICARE coverage, making it important to investigate this option before or immediately after a divorce becomes final.

Military spouses preparing for a change in coverage may also want to gather medical records, understand prescription needs and compare future insurance costs before existing coverage ends.

What Happens to Children's TRICARE After Divorce?

Divorce generally does not end TRICARE eligibility for the service member's biological or adopted children. However, stepchildren who were not adopted by the service member can lose their TRICARE eligibility when the divorce becomes final.

Custody arrangements and where children will live can also affect which TRICARE plan makes the most sense after divorce. Parents should review children's coverage separately from the former spouse's eligibility.

Why Planning Ahead Matters

Decisions about health insurance are part of the broader financial issues involved in a military divorce. When evaluating future medical coverage, military families should also understand:

Child support obligations

Military retirement benefits

Housing allowances

Property division

Parenting responsibilities

Looking at these issues together may help families prepare for life after divorce instead of addressing each issue separately.

How The Carlson Law Firm Helps Military Families

Military divorce often involves questions that extend beyond child custody and property division. Understanding how divorce may affect TRICARE, military benefits and future financial planning can help families make decisions before finalizing a divorce.

The Carlson Law Firm works with military families throughout Fort Hood, Killeen, Temple, Copperas Cove and Central Texas. Our family law attorneys help military spouses and service members better understand how Texas law and military regulations can affect divorce and related benefits.

text:
Texas licensed counselor Kevin D. Curry was found guilty by a federal jury in Fort Worth. Prosecutors stated he falsely billed the military healthcare TRICARE for transcranial magnetic stimulation treatments through three clinics, claiming over $26 million, while only about $17 million was actually paid out.

Curry, 64, operated Acuity TMS of Plano, Acuity TMS of Fort Worth, and Emerald Coast TMS of Fort Walton Beach in Florida. The charges spanned from September 2022 to the end of 2025. He is not a physician but presented himself as one to patients and used real doctors' credentials without their knowledge, instructing staff to forge treatment records.

To create billable treatment consent, he paid over $5.5 million in kickbacks to active-duty military personnel, veterans, and their families. Some recipients did not meet the criteria for TMS, and some never received treatment. TMS is used for severe depression and stimulates nerve cells using magnetic fields. The jury found him guilty of three counts of healthcare fraud, three counts of illegal kickbacks, and three counts of money laundering. Each count carries a maximum sentence of ten years, with sentencing dates yet to be determined.

The illicit funds were used for luxury hotels, expensive furniture, casino-themed parties for employees and beneficiaries, and a gold-plated Tesla Cybertruck. The Department of Justice stated the vehicle costs over $100,000; FBI seizure documents valued the 2024 model at approximately $73,230. The vehicle was seized on January 21, 2026, with about $200,000 in recovered assets, including approximately $136,000 in cash. The Department of Justice released a photo of the vehicle.

The buying side was driven by kickbacks and beneficiaries whose bills were paid by federal programs; the selling side involved packaging high-priced neurostimulation projects into the TRICARE clinic network. Funds flowed from the Department of Defense healthcare to clinic accounts, then into hotels, parties, and vehicles. The event was driven by federal prosecution and guilty verdicts, not market transactions. Beneficiaries include prosecutors who have seized some assets; the burden falls on military families' healthcare that was exploited and the doctors whose names were misused.

Source: Public Information

Curry did not invent new therapies but embedded existing, high-reimbursement TMS into military family channels. Clinics were established in military-populated North Texas and Florida's Walton Beach, first addressing "who qualifies for payment by the plan," then using kickbacks to resolve "who is willing to sign the bills." Misusing doctor credentials and falsifying medical records was to ensure the reimbursement system would still pay out without real physician oversight.

The capital path is short: TRICARE pays per project, clinics treat kickbacks as customer acquisition costs, with the remainder going to personal consumption. $5.5 million bought traffic, $17 million returned, with the difference becoming a lifestyle. This parallels the North American federal healthcare arbitrage chain where difficult-to-verify projects are easily turned into assembly lines.

Similar precedents include opioid prescription mills, genetic testing kickbacks, and compound pharmacy scams—all exploiting federal or employer plans as deep pockets, treating patients as billing vehicles. The industry remains in an expansion phase of payment loopholes rather than breakthroughs in treatment technology. The gold-plated pickup became a prosecutor's exhibit because luxury items are more visible to juries than medical records.

This reflects a misalignment of pricing power before regulatory changes. Treatment prices are determined by reimbursement schedules, not efficacy; whoever can control both customer acquisition and coding can bill for a magnetic stimulation session far exceeding costs. The mechanism is that military healthcare must cover mental health, with verification lagging behind multiple clinics and interstate billing, while kickbacks rewrite patients from being sick to becoming channels. The guilty verdict recovers symbolic items, not the majority of payments already spent.

text:
The New York Times: V.A. Institutes New Consent Requirements For Some Psychiatric Drugs

The Department of Veterans Affairs announced new measures on Monday that will require written informed consent by patients before they are prescribed certain psychiatric drugs. The shift reflects a growing disenchantment with psychotropic medications that has animated the Make America Healthy Again movement and its chief standard-bearer, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. (Ghorayshi and Jacobs, 9/28)

More news about veterans' healthcare —

Military.com: Ohio Veterans Are Paying 'Claim Sharks' Thousands For VA Benefits They Could Get For Free

Unaccredited companies are reportedly charging Ohio veterans thousands of dollars to file VA disability claims for assistance veterans could receive for free. “Claims sharks” charge veterans to prepare and file disability claims, sometimes for far more than the resulting benefits are worth, while promising results. That is even though federal law requires paid representatives to be accredited and generally bars charging veterans for help with an initial claim. (Gramegna, 9/29)

Military.com: Mental Health Counselor Convicted In $26 Million Tricare Fraud And Kickback Scheme

A jury has convicted the owner of a Texas mental health clinic for a $26 million TRICARE fraud, kickback and money laundering scheme. Licensed professional counselor Kevin Curry, 64, of Frisco, Texas, was found guilty Sept. 24 in Fort Worth of health care fraud, kickbacks and money laundering, according to the Department of Justice. The jury convicted Curry of three counts of health care fraud, three counts of offering and paying illegal health care kickbacks, and three counts of engaging in monetary transactions in criminal derived property. (Mordowanec, 9/29)

In other developments from the Trump administration —

Politico: Vance, RFK Jr. And 'Iron' Mike To Headline MAHA Summit

Vice President JD Vance and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. will speak for the second year in a row Tuesday at an event organized by Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again allies in Washington. Vance and Kennedy will close the all-day event with a “fireside chat,” according to the agenda. They will talk about MAHA’s “accomplishments, its regulatory reform agenda and its priorities for the year ahead,” according to the organizers. (Paun, 9/28)

AP: Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court To Allow Restrictions On Transgender Inmates' Medical Care

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to let it enforce, for now, restrictions on gender-affirming care in federal prison. The emergency appeal comes after lower courts blocked officials from immediately carrying out the policy adopted after an executive order from President Donald Trump. U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth ordered the government to continue providing gender-affirming care like hormone therapy. (Whitehurst, 9/28)

The Washington Post: Education Department Officially Scraps Biden-Era Title IX Rules

The Education Department will scrap Biden-era Title IX rules that sought to bolster nondiscrimination protections based on sexual orientation and gender identity, officials announced Monday, marking a return to rules from the first Trump administration. The regulations, initially released in 2020, outline how schools must handle reports of sexual misconduct, including setting a stricter definition for what constitutes sexual harassment and giving more due process rights to those accused. The rules, which take effect Tuesday, will not change much for schools. The Trump administration has been enforcing its own rules, including targeting schools that allow transgender athletes to play on girls’ and women’s sports teams, since the president took office last year. (Lumpkin, 9/28)

ProPublica: This White House Plan Threatens Funding For Disabled Voters

Without Amy Miller, some elderly and disabled people wouldn’t be able to vote. The attorney for Disability Rights Nebraska travels the state, investigating the quality of nursing homes and assisted living facilities. As she reminds the residents how they can report abuse or neglect, she also offers voter registration forms. Last month, she helped a veteran with a traumatic brain injury fill out change-of-address paperwork so he could vote in the upcoming midterm elections. “He 100% knew who he wanted to vote for,” Miller said, but he struggled to write with a pen. (Song, 9/29)

Health news from Capitol Hill —

The Hill: Senate Majority PAC Launches $2M Ad Campaign Targeting Sen. Susan Collins Over Medicaid Cuts

A Democratic super PAC on Monday launched a new ad campaign attacking Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) for the closure of about a dozen birthing centers in Maine, arguing she helped enable the massive Medicaid cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act even though she voted against the legislation. The Senate Majority PAC, which supports efforts to establish a Democratic majority in the Senate, announced a $2 million ad campaign to air across Maine, tying her vote to advance the One Big Beautiful Bill Act last year to the closure of birthing centers in Maine. (Choi, 9/28)

Stat: Midterm Election: Washington Insiders See Policy Changes Coming

Health industry leaders, still contending with the new rules of President Trump’s Washington, are about to face another shift. November’s midterm elections are likely to shake up key health policy debates, from Medicaid funding to the price of medication. That’s especially true if Democrats seize control of a chamber of Congress, though any major policymaking would still need Trump’s signature. (Payne, 9/29)

title: AFA Grant Supports New Military Families in Nebraska - Air & Space Forces Association
description:
The Air & Space Forces Association Lincoln Chapter and the Nebraska Air National Guard Family Support Office, with the generous support of an AFA United Forces & Families grant, jointly sponsored a baby shower for recent and expecting parents of the Nebraska National Guard.
The baby shower—held on August 22 in Bellevue, Neb.—directly supported Nebraska Air National Guard members who support critical missions and operations at Offutt Air Force Base.
Recognizing and supporting new and future families is key to retaining members in military units, including the Nebraska Air National Guard, and to ensuring every family member feels part of the service community.
Supporting military families—especially during major life milestones like childbirth—reinforces the vital role families play in mission success.
On behalf of Offutt’s expecting families, the Nebraska Air National Guard and the AFA Lincoln Chapter thank AFA’s United Forces & Families Program and the grant that helped make the event possible and so memorable for the parents.
text:
The Air & Space Forces Association Lincoln Chapter and the Nebraska Air National Guard Family Support Office, with the generous support of an AFA United Forces & Families grant, jointly sponsored a baby shower for recent and expecting parents of the Nebraska National Guard. The baby shower—held on August 22 in Bellevue, Neb.—directly supported Nebraska Air National Guard members who support critical missions and operations at Offutt Air Force Base.

The afternoon provided an enjoyable social environment for the soon-to-be parents, featuring refreshments and the gifting of essential care supplies for newborns. AFA and the Family Support Office also offered educational and wellness resources for the periods before, during, and after pregnancy, including Postpartum Fitness, TRICARE and DEERS information, financial planning, and access to new parent programs.

Recognizing and supporting new and future families is key to retaining members in military units, including the Nebraska Air National Guard, and to ensuring every family member feels part of the service community. Supporting military families—especially during major life milestones like childbirth—reinforces the vital role families play in mission success.

On behalf of Offutt’s expecting families, the Nebraska Air National Guard and the AFA Lincoln Chapter thank AFA’s United Forces & Families Program and the grant that helped make the event possible and so memorable for the parents. Events like these serve as a reminder that to retain a service member, the family must be retained first.
